faq.a: Acetyl‑CoA cannot be generated from fatty acids, so hepatic ketogenesis is minimal.
faq.q: Why are ketones low in a beta‑oxidation defect?

faq.a: No; without carnitine fatty acids cannot enter mitochondria, leading to energy failure.
faq.q: Can a patient survive without carnitine?

faq.a: Only if combined with adequate carbohydrate intake; otherwise it worsens energy deficit.

exam: A 6‑month‑old presents after a prolonged fast with seizures and low glucose; ketones are absent. – Identify the metabolic block and immediate management.
Explain why malonyl‑CoA levels fall during fasting and how this affects CPT‑I activity. – Show understanding of regulation.
A patient on valproate develops hypoglycaemia; what secondary metabolic pathway is likely impaired? – Link drug effect to beta‑oxidation.
Differentiate MCAD deficiency from glycogen storage disease type I based on laboratory findings. – Compare ketone and lactate patterns.
In a malaria‑endemic region, a child with fever and vomiting becomes lethargic; what metabolic complication should you consider and why? – Apply tropical context.
Describe the stepwise reactions of one cycle of beta‑oxidation and the cofactors produced. – Test pathway knowledge.

A newborn screen shows elevated C8 acyl‑carnitine; what is the most likely diagnosis and next confirmatory test? – Interpret screening result.
ai.title: Beta Oxidation of Fatty Acids
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Beta oxidation breaks down fatty acids in mitochondria to acetyl‑CoA for the citric acid cycle, providing energy during fasting or prolonged exercise. Key control is CPT‑I, and defects cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and cardiomyopathy, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Occurs in mitochondria after fatty acids are activated and transported via the carnitine shuttle.
Provides most ATP during fasting, prolonged exercise, and in newborns.
sections.p: Beta oxidation is the stepwise removal of two‑carbon units from fatty acids within the mitochondrial matrix, yielding acetyl‑CoA, NADH and FADH2 for ATP production.

b: Acyl‑CoA dehydrogenase creates a trans‑Δ²‑enoyl‑CoA and FADH2.
Enoyl‑CoA hydratase adds water → L‑hydroxyacyl‑CoA.
Hydroxyacyl‑CoA dehydrogenase forms β‑ketoacyl‑CoA and NADH.
β‑ketoacyl‑CoA thiolase releases acetyl‑CoA and a shortened acyl‑CoA.
sections.p: Long‑chain fatty acids are activated to acyl‑CoA, shuttled into mitochondria by CPT‑I (outer membrane) and CPT‑II (inner membrane), then undergo four recurring reactions each cycle.

b: High insulin → ↑ malonyl‑CoA → CPT‑I inhibition → ↓ oxidation.
Fasting → ↓ insulin, ↑ glucagon → ↓ malonyl‑CoA → CPT‑I activation.
sections.p: The rate‑limiting step is CPT‑I, inhibited by malonyl‑CoA (fatty acid synthesis signal) and activated when insulin is low and glucagon high.

b: CPT‑I deficiency – severe infantile hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly.
Medium‑chain acyl‑CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (MCAD) – fasting intolerance, sudden death.
Secondary inhibition by valproate, carnitine deficiency (malnutrition, chronic alcoholism).
sections.p: Inherited enzyme deficiencies or secondary inhibition (e.g., drugs, malnutrition) impair beta oxidation, leading to energy failure, hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, and organ dysfunction.

b: Check for fasting history, recent infection, or drug exposure.
Look for hepatomegaly, cardiomyopathy, and low ketones despite hypoglycaemia.
sections.p: Patients present with lethargy, vomiting, seizures after a period of fasting or illness. In low‑resource settings, infections (malaria, HIV) increase metabolic demand and precipitate crises.
When acyl‑carnitine analysis is unavailable, rely on clinical fasting test (monitor glucose, ketones) and treat empirically.

t.b: Identifies specific enzyme blocks; accumulation of characteristic chain‑length species confirms diagnosis.
Hypoglycaemia with low/absent ketones suggests beta‑oxidation defect.
Low free carnitine supports secondary deficiency; treat with supplementation.
Detects ventricular dysfunction caused by energy deficit.

b: IV glucose (10% dextrose) to raise blood sugar and suppress fatty‑acid oxidation.
Avoid fasting; give frequent carbohydrate‑rich meals.
Carnitine supplementation if deficiency confirmed.
Avoid valproate and other fatty‑acid oxidation inhibitors.
Treat precipitating infection aggressively (e.g., malaria, TB, HIV opportunistic infections).
sections.p: Immediate goal is to stop catabolism and provide alternative fuel; long‑term care prevents recurrence.

b: Glycogen storage disease type I – also causes hypoglycaemia but with high ketones.
Organic acidemias – present with metabolic acidosis and elevated anion gap.
Normal ketones in early MCAD crisis; repeat testing after a short fast.
Low carnitine may be secondary to malnutrition, not primary deficiency.
Key control point: CPT‑I inhibited by malonyl‑CoA.
MCAD is the most common fatty‑acid oxidation disorder worldwide.
In low‑resource settings, always consider infection‑triggered crisis.

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of heart failure or severe hepatomegaly
